slides.text: As chief conservator at the National Gallery, I spend my nights in a lead-lined basement scanning seventeenth-century oil paintings with infrared reflectography. Old masters couldn't afford to waste linen; when a patron failed to pay, the artist simply painted a new nobleman over the old one. Last week, the museum director personally locked me in the vault with a newly acquired 1648 Dutch portrait.

The surface canvas showed a burgomaster in a lace collar. The carbon-14 dating on the oak frame and lead-white pigment was indisputably three hundred and eighty years old. But as the infrared camera stitched together the hidden layer beneath the varnish, the burgomaster dissolved—revealing a second figure painted in the same centuries-old lead pigment underneath.

It was a woman bound to a chair in a windowless concrete room—this very vault—staring in terror past the painter's easel. In the corner of the underpainting, rendered in flawless seventeenth-century brushwork, stood our museum director checking a modern stainless-steel wristwatch. Behind me, the heavy vault door clicked as the keypad was disabled from the outside.
